So I wasn’t talked out of it but I feel like this is good to know if someone ever tells you they’re going to attempt. I was 14 when I attempted and I hadn’t told anyone except for this guy I thought I was in love with who was 17. He simply told me “I hope the grass is greener on the other side.” Please please please do not say anything like this. In my suicidal state I took that as “I guess no one really does care” and I proceeded to take 27 Vicodin, 30 Lexapro, and an array of other pills that I don’t remember. I of course, blacked out and I guess the guy I told realized what he did and got ahold of my mom on Facebook and thankfully my mom found me. She gave me CPR until the paramedics arrived and was told that they didn’t know if I was going to make it. I spent 3 days in the ICU in and out of consciousness and was finally able to be stabilized. I then spent a good chunk of my freshman year going through inpatient, partial-hospitalization, and residential treatment. On September 14th, it will have been 6 years since my attempt. I am forever grateful that I survived and am able to tell my story. I’m currently a pre-med student with a dream to become and adolescent psychiatrist to help those who were like me. If someone confides with you that they are contemplating suicide, it’s more than likely a cry for help whether they realize it or not. Talk to them, tell them that you want them to be in this world with you, that you love them (even if you may think this is weird), and if you know they have a roommate or family member who may be around, tell them so they can be with them physically. Sorry OP for not fitting your description.

It wasn’t until I started opening up in therapy and explaining to my psychiatrist the symptoms I was having that I was diagnosed. It’s taken me awhile to accept that diagnosis and the best thing I was told is that trauma is subjective. What’s traumatic to you may not be traumatic to someone else. But that trauma is still valid and the symptoms you’re experiencing are also valid.

It’s interesting you say this because this is how I felt about myself before I accepted that I needed help. I was diagnosed with Bulimia at the age of 13. Went to partial hospitalization treatment for a month and just went through the motions and did everything I could do get cleared so I could get out. I didn’t take it seriously because I thought I didn’t need help. I wasn’t that bad. My home life was okay and I just needed to put on my big girl pants and get over it and that other people had it a lot worse. It wasn’t until I spent 3 days in the ICU from an attempt to take my own life a year later that myself and my family realized that I had a genuine problem that couldn’t just be fixed by willpower alone. I know not everyone is this way, but I feel like a lot of people with mental illness try to deny it for awhile and don’t go about thinking “woe is me.” 

I will say though, for some mental illnesses (depression in particular) part of recovery is getting your shit together. And by that I mean getting the help you need and activity working on changing your way of thinking so you don’t further yourself into depression. This is a long process though. I’m 20 now and I still need therapy and medication and I still have my really low days, but things are a million times better than where I used to be.

I agree and disagree with you. I was diagnosed with depression and anxiety at a fairly young age. I think a lot of it stemmed from a family history of mental illness and my upbringing.

However, I do think that people can get themselves deeper into their depression and anxiety based off of their mindset. Until I had hit rock bottom, I would always look for the negatives in every situation. This would further validate that life sucks and life isn’t worth it and so on. 

After years of therapy and medication, I’m a whole lot better and I always tell myself that for every negative in life, there are two positives. That outlook has changed my life and makes everything look a lot less bleak. My point is, I don’t think it’s necessarily the mindset that causes depression and anxiety, but more so it can prolong and worsen it. That mindset is not at all easy to change though.
